name: Herbie Hancock
description: Herbie Hancock, born April 12, 1940, in Chicago, performed a Mozart concerto with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra at age 11. In 1963 he joined the Miles Davis Quintet, staying five years and helping redefine the jazz rhythm section. He also performed at Chicago's Regal Theater. His 1973 Columbia album Head Hunters — made with the Headhunters band of Bennie Maupin, Paul Jackson, Harvey Mason, and Bill Summers — became the best-selling jazz album of its era, on the strength of the fifteen-minute "Chameleon" and a ground-up rebuild of "Watermelon Man," proving the synthesizer belonged in Black music's vanguard. He received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 2004.

name: Harold Washington
description: Harold Washington (April 15, 1922 – November 25, 1987), born in Chicago and raised in Bronzeville, was the first Black mayor of Chicago. His earlier service is documented in the Harold Washington Archives & Collections at the Harold Washington Library Center, which hold his State Representative records (1957–1976) and Congressional records (1970–1983). He was elected mayor on April 12, 1983, and took office on April 29, 1983; his campaign was powered in part by Black radio — journalist Lu Palmer's "Lu's Notebook" on WVON and the "We Shall See in '83" drive are graded VERIFIED in CTL's media dossier as pivotal to the election. Washington's first term was dominated by the racially polarized Council Wars, in which a 29-alderman majority on the City Council battled his administration and blocked much of its agenda. He was reelected in April 1987 and died in office on November 25, 1987, of a heart attack in his City Hall office. The Harold Washington Library Center and the DuSable Museum's Harold Washington Wing (added 1993) carry his institutional legacy.

name: Hard Again
description: Hard Again is the 1977 comeback album by Chicago blues master Muddy Waters, released on Blue Sky Records on January 10, 1977. After Chess Records — Waters' label home for a quarter-century — folded in 1975, the Texas guitarist Johnny Winter, a lifelong Waters admirer, brought him back into the studio, producing the album and playing guitar alongside members of Waters' road band: James Cotton on harmonica, Pinetop Perkins on piano, Bob Margolin on guitar and Willie “Big Eyes” Smith on drums. Winter set out to recreate the raw force of Waters' 1950s Chess recordings, and the album — opening with a thunderous re-recording of “Mannish Boy” — was hailed by AllMusic as one of the finest Waters ever made. It won the Grammy Award for Best Ethnic or Traditional Folk Recording and opened a late-career renaissance that produced two more Winter-produced studio albums.

name: Head Hunters
description: Head Hunters is Herbie Hancock's 1973 album for Columbia Records, co-produced by David Rubinson, and a defining document of jazz-funk fusion. Its four extended tracks — 'Chameleon,' 'Watermelon Man,' 'Sly,' and 'Vein Melter' — pair jazz improvisation with funk and R&B rhythms, with Hancock on Fender Rhodes, clavinet, and ARP synthesizers alongside reedman Bennie Maupin, bassist Paul Jackson, drummer Harvey Mason, and percussionist Bill Summers. 'Watermelon Man' is a new electric arrangement of the composition from Hancock's 1962 debut, Takin' Off, and 'Sly' honors Sly Stone, one of the funk musicians — with James Brown and Curtis Mayfield — whose example Hancock absorbed. Released in October 1973, the album sold more than a million copies, became the first platinum-selling jazz record, and was for a time the best-selling jazz album ever; the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry in 2007.

name: Harry Belafonte
description: Harry Belafonte (born Harold George Bellanfanti Jr., March 1, 1927, Harlem, New York, to Jamaican immigrant parents; died April 25, 2023, New York City, of congestive heart failure, aged 96) was the singer and actor who carried calypso to the world and bankrolled the civil rights movement from inside it. Partly raised in Jamaica, he served in the U.S. Navy in the Second World War and trained at the Dramatic Workshop alongside Sidney Poitier. He won a Tony Award in 1954 for John Murray Anderson's Almanac, recorded for RCA Victor from the early 1950s, and his “Matilda” (1953) opened the calypso wave. His album Calypso (1956), home of “Day-O (The Banana Boat Song),” was the first LP by a single artist to sell one million copies and spent thirty-one weeks atop the Billboard chart; by 1959 he was the highest-paid Black performer in history. His films include Bright Road (1953), Carmen Jones (1954), Island in the Sun (1957), and a final appearance in BlacKkKlansman (2018). He was a close ally of Martin Luther King Jr. and a movement financier across six decades.

name: Harlem Renaissance
description: The Harlem Renaissance was the great flowering of Black literature, music, theater, and visual art centered in Harlem, New York, during the 1920s — the era the intake timeline anchors at 1920. Fed by the Great Migration and by a generation determined to define Black identity in its own voice, the movement produced Langston Hughes (CTL-E-0338), Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, and Jean Toomer in letters; Duke Ellington and the Cotton Club era in music; and a visual language carried by Aaron Douglas and Augusta Savage. Its manifesto moment came in 1925 with Alain Locke's anthology The New Negro, which framed the movement as a spiritual and cultural emancipation to match the political one still being fought. The Renaissance was never only Harlem's — its writers and musicians circulated through Chicago, Washington, and Paris — but Harlem was its capital and its symbol. The graph holds many of its people one by one; this record holds the movement itself, so the era can be cited as an era and not only as a shelf of biographies.

name: Hal Jackson
description: Trailblazing Black sportscaster and DJ (Washington, DC; New York). First African American radio sports announcer (1939); host of The Bronze Review on WINX; co-founder of Inner City Broadcasting (1971) with Percy Sutton; first minority inducted into the NAB Hall of Fame (1990); first Black inductee into the National Radio Hall of Fame (1995); Guinness record 73-year broadcast career. Died May 23, 2012, New York City, age 96.

name: Hazel B. Garland
description: Journalist and editor (January 28, 1913 - April 5, 1988); the first African American woman editor-in-chief of a nationally circulated newspaper chain (New Pittsburgh Courier, from 1974); wrote the pioneering TV column 'Video Vignettes' from 1955; NNPA Editor of the Year 1974; Pulitzer juror 1978-1979.

name: Houston Defender
description: Houston Black weekly newspaper founded October 11, 1930 by Clifton F. Richardson Sr. (editor/publisher); part of Houston's multi-paper Black press ecosystem; now the Houston Defender Network under publisher/CEO Sonny Messiah-Jiles.

name: Houston Forward Times
description: Houston Black weekly newspaper opened in 1960 by Julius P. Carter; a three-generation family paper (Julius Carter - Lenora 'Doll' Carter - Karen Carter Richards), still publishing under CEO/Publisher Karen Carter Richards.

name: HBCU Radio Archives
description: Preservation program for the broadcast archives of 29 HBCU radio stations (of 104 HBCUs nationwide): reel-to-reel, cassettes, and obsolete digital media, some already at risk of loss. Funded by the Mellon Foundation's $5M grant to WYSO (2024); a WYSO Archives + NEDCC collaboration led by founding director Jocelyn Robinson. Reformatted material goes to the American Archive of Public Broadcasting; oral histories to Jackson State's Margaret Walker Center.

name: Hurricane Katrina - Calhoun-McCormick archive flooded
description: August 2005: New Orleans photographers Keith Calhoun and Chandra McCormick evacuate their Lower Ninth Ward home/studio for Hurricane Katrina; returning more than two months later, they find two-thirds of their 30-year photographic archive destroyed by water damage. The salvaged work becomes the 'Right to Return' series.

name: HBCU Radio Preservation Project $5M grant
description: January 2024: the Mellon Foundation awarded $5M to community-owned WYSO (Yellow Springs, Ohio) to preserve the radio archives of 29 HBCU stations, a collaboration between the WYSO Archives and the Northeast Document Conservation Center (NEDCC), led by founding director Jocelyn Robinson. Builds on two earlier grant programs; field archivist funded through December 31, 2027.

name: Hansberry v. Lee, 311 U.S. 32 (1940)
description: U.S. Supreme Court decision (311 U.S. 32; argued Oct 25, 1940; decided Nov 12, 1940) holding res judicata did not bar a new challenge to a Woodlawn racially restrictive covenant: the covenant required 95% frontage-owner signatures but only about 54% had signed, so dissenters were inadequately represented in Burke v. Kleiman (1934). Argued by Earl B. Dickerson for Carl Augustus Hansberry; cracked the covenant system and opened the road to Shelley v. Kraemer (1948).

name: HOLC Residential Security Map — Chicago Area D74
aliases: Chicago HOLC Area D74; D74 (Chicago HOLC)
description: Area D74 is a numbered district on the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's 1940 Residential Security Map of Chicago, graded D ('Hazardous'). The Chicago map's D grades tracked Black and immigrant neighborhoods with explicitly racialized survey language; Federal Reserve research (2017) links placement on the lower-graded side of HOLC boundaries to long-run reductions in homeownership, house values, and rents.

name: Hyde Park Township
description: Former civil township in Cook County, Illinois — a separate municipality from 1861 until its annexation into Chicago in 1889. Created by the Illinois General Assembly in 1861, it stretched from Pershing Road (39th Street) to 138th Street and the Calumet River, State Street to Lake Michigan and the Indiana state line — much of what is now Chicago's South Side. In the June 29, 1889 elections the township's voters (population ~85,000) approved annexation. After annexation the 'Hyde Park' neighborhood name narrowed to the historic core between 51st and 55th Streets near the lakefront.

name: Hansberry house (6140 S. Rhodes)
description: In Hansberry v. Lee (1940), the U.S.

name: HOLC redlining — 63rd Street corridor (areas incl. D74)
description: HOLC graded large parts of Chicago's South Side, including the Black Belt, D ('hazardous'). Area D74 ran from 35th to 67th Street between State Street and Cottage Grove — the heart of the Black Belt, including Bronzeville and Washington Park. Its area description discusses restricting 'the colored people' via real-estate protective associations and cites Washington Park as 'almost completely monopolized by the colored race' as rationale for the grade; it also flags the Ida B. Wells housing project for 'unsettling patterns of tradition.' Public housing built in Chicago from the 1930s to the 1960s was largely located in HOLC 'hazardous' neighborhoods.

name: Harry's Show Lounge
description: 63rd Street show lounge at 432 E. 63rd St. (1947-1963) in Woodlawn; early-career Ramsey Lewis Trio appearances June 6 & 18, 1956 (with George 'Stardust' Greene and Eldee Young); also the Johnny Pate trio (1955), Les Tucker Trio (1958), and the Rhythm Aces (1958).

name: Hillman's (grocery)
aliases: Hillman's Pure Foods; Hillman's Food Stores
description: Chicago grocery chain with stores across Chicagoland (early 1960s: 13+ locations); operated groceries in the basements of Wieboldt's and Sears in Englewood and ran the 70,000 sq ft Hillman's Bakery at 3853 W. 43rd St.

name: Harrison's Barber Shop
description: Long-running Woodlawn barbershop at 6437 S. Cottage Grove Ave., owned 15 years by Davis (a Woodlawn resident since 1972) before closing for building rehabilitation; cited as an example of Black small-business persistence through Woodlawn's disinvestment.

name: Halsted CTA station (Green Line)
description: CTA 'L' station at 6321 S Halsted St, Englewood, Chicago. Opened December 24, 1906 on the Englewood branch (renamed the Ashland branch); elevated, 2 side platforms; rebuilt 1927 and 1996; the only remaining intermediate station on the 3.1-mile Ashland branch.

name: Harvard CTA station site (Green Line)
description: Former Englewood-branch 'L' station at 303 W. 63rd St. (Harvard Ave. and 63rd) in Englewood: opened November 3, 1906; northern terminus of the Normal Park branch (May 25, 1907 - Jan 29, 1954); closed February 9, 1992, in CTA budget cuts; demolished during the 1994-96 Green Line reconstruction; a federally funded replacement was never built.

name: Henry Blair
description: Inventor (1807-1860); the second African American U.S. patent holder: U.S. Patent X8447 (October 14, 1834) for a seed planter, plus an 1836 cotton-planter patent. Unable to read or write, he signed his patent with an X; Patent Office records identified him as 'a colored man' - the only inventor so identified.

name: Henry T. Sampson Jr.
description: Nuclear engineer and inventor (April 22, 1934 - June 4, 2015); the first African American Ph.D. in nuclear engineering in the U.S. (UIUC, 1967); co-inventor with George H. Miley of the gamma-electric cell (U.S. Patent 3,591,860, July 6, 1971); China Lake and Aerospace Corporation career; also a noted Black film historian whose collection went to Jackson State University in 2011.

name: Half-Century Magazine
description: Anthony Overton's Black lifestyle magazine (1916–1925), named for the 50th anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation; Katherine E. Williams was listed as owner and editor-in-chief. It was the precursor to Overton's Chicago Bee.

name: Hermene Hartman
description: Media pioneer (born September 24, 1947, Chicago); founder of the N'DIGO magapaper (1989); former vice chancellor of the City Colleges of Chicago (first woman in the role); began at Operation Breadbasket coordinating the Black Expo; WBBM-TV public-service producer; operator of The Hartman Group PR firm since 1977.

name: Hiram E. Jackson
description: Chief executive officer of Detroit-based Real Times Media, whose holdings include the Chicago Defender, Michigan Chronicle, New Pittsburgh Courier, Atlanta Daily World, and Tri-State Defender; in July 2019 he moved the Chicago Defender to digital-only after 114 years of print.

name: House music — name origin
aliases: origin of the term 'house music'; house music etymology
description: The contested origin of the genre name 'house music': the consensus derivation is from the Warehouse nightclub at 206 S. Jefferson Street (relocated there in 1977; city landmark 2023), where Frankie Knuckles was resident DJ from March 1977 — patrons called it 'the House' and asked for 'house music.' Documented transmission mechanisms include Imports Etc.'s record bins labeled 'As Heard at the Warehouse' (shortened to 'House'), a tavern sign Knuckles saw c. 1980–81, and rival claims by Farley 'Jackmaster' Funk (imports) and Larry Heard (home production).

name: Hales Franciscan High School
description: Black Catholic college-preparatory high school in Bronzeville at 4930 S Cottage Grove Ave (1962-2019): the only historically African American, all-male Catholic college-prep school in Illinois. Opened by the Franciscan Province of the Sacred Heart; part of the Archdiocese of Chicago. Alumni include JaVale McGee (2006) and Jerome Randle (2006). Campus acquired November 6, 2023 by It Takes A Village Family of Schools.

name: Highland Community Bank
description: Black-owned community bank on Chicago's South Side (1970-2015); closed January 23, 2015 by Illinois regulators for operating in an unsafe and unsound condition with inadequate capital; all deposits assumed by United Fidelity Bank of Evansville, Indiana.

name: Howalton Day School
description: Black private nonsectarian school on Chicago's South Side, founded 1946 by three Black educators — June Howe-White, Doris Allen-Anderson, and Charlotte B. Stratton (the name combines their surnames) — and operating until 1986. Chicago's oldest African American private nonsectarian school, founded as a CPS-critical alternative stressing discovery, creativity, the arts, and humanities; its archives (9 linear feet) are held at the Chicago Public Library's Woodson Regional Library / Harsh Research Collection. Exemplifies Black Chicago's 'dual educational agenda' (Hayes 2010).

name: Homegoing service
aliases: home-going service; Black homegoing; homegoing celebration
description: The African-American Christian funeral tradition framing death as a celebratory 'going home' to the Lord — gospel music, elaborate printed programs, open casket, expressive grief, and the repast — rooted in enslavement-era hush harbors where the enslaved fused African tradition with Christianity in secret, and in the Black church. Homegoings also became explicitly political, from Emmett Till's open-casket funeral to movement funerals, and an economic engine: Black funeral directors became major Reconstruction-era business figures.

name: Hall Branch Library and Vivian Harsh Collection
description: Bronzeville branch of the Chicago Public Library where Vivian G. Harsh — the first African American to run a CPL branch — built the 'Special Negro Collection' from 1932, modeled on the Schomburg Center, Fisk University Library, and Atlanta University Library collections. With children's librarian Charlemae Hill Rollins (first at the branch, thirty years of service), the collection became an engine of the Chicago Renaissance, drawing support from Richard Wright, Margaret Walker, Arna Bontemps, Gwendolyn Brooks, Langston Hughes, and Horace Cayton. Neglected for a decade after Harsh's 1958 retirement, it was revived by an $89,000 federal grant in 1970 with a full-time curator, renamed the Vivian G. Harsh Collection of Afro-American History and Literature, and moved to the Carter G. Woodson Regional Library in 1975 — today the oldest and largest African American studies repository in the Midwest.

name: Hair-care routines at home
aliases: hot-comb pressing at home; kitchen beauticians
description: Everyday domestic Black beauty labor: hot-comb pressing and relaxers at home in the 1950s-60s; Johnson Products' Ultra Sheen (1957) replaced the hot comb for many; the Afro Sheen era of natural hair in the 1970s. A hot comb is preserved at the Smithsonian NMAAHC as an artifact of everyday Black life.

name: House parties and basement parties — ordinary Black nightlife
aliases: basement parties; house party circuit; Black Chicago house parties
description: Neighborhood house parties as the base layer of Black Chicago nightlife: DJs in living rooms and basements charging a few dollars at the door, social-club dances, union-hall parties — the underground circuit that grew because mainstream clubs excluded Black and gay patrons, and the seedbed from which both Chicago house music and the footwork dance battle scene grew.

name: Hair-product objects: Ultra Wave -> Ultra Sheen -> Afro Sheen
aliases: Ultra Wave; Ultra Sheen; Afro Sheen
description: The Johnson Products Company product lineage - Ultra Wave (1954) to Ultra Sheen (1957) to Afro Sheen: Chicago's Black hair-care empire, the first African-American-owned company traded on the American Stock Exchange (1971) and first Black sponsor of a national TV program (Soul Train).

name: Hot comb / pressing comb
description: Heated metal comb for straightening hair; a multi-inventor history - Marcel Grateau (late 1800s France), Walter Sammons (U.S. patent 1,362,823, Dec 21 1920), Elroy J. Duncan; commonly but wrongly attributed to Madam C.J. Walker.

name: Harold Washington 1982-83 Voter Registration Drive
description: Church-anchored voter registration campaign preceding Harold Washington's 1983 mayoral run: his summer-1982 pledge (50,000 new voters), the 'Come Alive, October 5' / 'We Shall See in '83' slogan, the Task Force for Black Political Empowerment and Operation PUSH; 100,000-200,000+ new Black voters registered in months. Washington announced November 10, 1982, won April 12, 1983, and was inaugurated April 29, 1983, as Chicago's first Black mayor.

description: Practice-squad stop from Nov 4, 2009

name: Huber Heights, Ohio
description: Freeman's hometown; Wayne High School

name: Hurd v. Hodge (1948)
description: U.S. Supreme Court case (1948), companion to Shelley v. Kraemer, argued by Charles H. Houston, barring judicial enforcement of racial covenants in the District of Columbia.

name: Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged
description: Auburn, New York home for aged and indigent Black people, established on land Tubman donated to the AME Zion Church in 1903; opened 1908.

name: Harriet Tubman
description: Underground Railroad conductor known as “Moses”; Union Army scout, spy, and nurse; led the 1863 Combahee River Raid; founded the Harriet Tubman Home for the Aged in Auburn, New York.

name: Henry Highland Garnet
description: Abolitionist Presbyterian minister; delivered the 1843 “Address to the Slaves of the United States”; first Black American to address the U.S. House of Representatives (1865); U.S. Minister to Liberia.

description: 1916 Tuskegee agricultural bulletin by George Washington Carver cataloguing uses for the peanut.

name: Harpo Studios
description: Oprah Winfrey's television production campus in Chicago's West Loop; home of The Oprah Winfrey Show from 1990 to 2011.

name: How to Succeed in Business Without Being White
description: Earl G. Graves Sr.'s 1997 business memoir and manual; a New York Times bestseller.

name: Henry McKee Minton
description: Philadelphia physician and pharmacist (1870-1946); co-founder of Sigma Pi Phi on May 15, 1904, and its first Grand Sire Archon; helped organize the Beta Boule in Chicago in 1907.

name: Horst Lippmann
description: German concert promoter (born March 17, 1927, in Eisenach; died May 18, 1997, in Dreieich). With Fritz Rau he established the concert agency Lippmann + Rau in 1962 and organized the first American Folk Blues Festival European tour. The pair's business materials form the Lippmann + Rau Music Archive (formerly the International Jazz Archive Eisenach).

name: Harry S. Truman
description: 33rd President of the United States (1945-1953). Alice Dunnigan accompanied his 1948 whistle-stop campaign tour, the first Black woman journalist on a presidential tour.

name: Haitian Pavilion (World's Columbian Exposition)
description: Haiti's national pavilion at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, built in Chicago's Jackson Park; dedicated January 2, 1893, with Frederick Douglass's 'Lecture on Haiti,' and used by Douglass and Ida B. Wells as offices for civil-rights advocacy during the fair.

name: Hot Mix 5
description: Chicago DJ crew chosen by WBMX program director Lee Michaels in 1981 as resident DJs of the "Saturday Night Live Ain’t No Jive" mix show; founding members Farley "Funkin" Keith (later Farley "Jackmaster" Funk), Mickey "Mixin" Oliver, Ralphi Rosario, Kenny "Jammin" Jason, and Scott "Smokin" Silz.

name: Hickory (Chesapeake), Virginia
description: Hickory, Virginia (now the city of Chesapeake): birthplace of Bessie Blount (November 24, 1914). She attended Diggs Chapel Elementary School there before her formal schooling ended at sixth grade and the family moved to New Jersey.

name: Horace M. Peterson III
description: Horace M. Peterson III (1945-1992) founded the Black Archives of Mid-America in 1974 after collecting African American artifacts since adolescence. His vision also drove the Kansas City Jazz Museum, the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum, and the restoration of the historic Gem Theater. He died in a drowning accident in March 1992 at age 46.

name: Hammond, Louisiana
description: Hammond is a city in Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana, and the home of Southeastern Louisiana University, a public university. The university's Center for Southeast Louisiana Studies, based in Hammond, preserves the history and cultures of Louisiana's Florida Parishes and surrounding areas, and maintains the Southeastern Louisiana University Archives and Special Collections, some 600 collections. Among the Center's custodial holdings are the records of the Richard Funeral Home of Lake Charles — the thread that brings Hammond into CultureTechLens's preservation research, which tracks the surviving records of Black funeral homes and the regional archives that hold them.

name: Harold Lucas
description: Bronzeville historian, preservationist, and community organizer; founder of the Black Metropolis Convention Visitor Center (1996) and president of the Black Metropolis Convention and Tourism Council.

name: Howard Stirk Holdings
description: Broadcast company led by Armstrong Williams; acquired WEYI-TV and WWMB-TV from Sinclair in 2013, growing to seven Black-owned stations (Pew 2016); stations operated under Sinclair shared-services agreements; FCC approved license transfers to Sinclair in September 2026.

name: Henry M. Leland
description: Detroit precision machinist and engineer who organized the Cadillac Automobile Company in August 1902 from the remnants of the Henry Ford Company; led Cadillac until 1917, then founded the Lincoln Motor Company.

description: Assistant state’s attorney who migrated from Augusta, Georgia; incorporator and 1919 president of the Cook County Bar Association; assigned to Harrison Street Police Court in 1921.

name: Hay
description: 1996 marijuana-themed hit single by Crucial Conflict, from The Final Tic; built on the group’s self-styled rapid-fire "rodeo" hip-hop sound.

name: Howard Vaughan
description: Husband of Dorothy Vaughan (married 1932; died 1955); the couple had six children.

name: Hidden Figures Congressional Gold Medal (2019)
description: Dorothy Vaughan is posthumously awarded the Congressional Gold Medal in 2019 for the Hidden Figures' contributions to the American space program.

name: Hidden Figures book published (2016)
description: Margot Lee Shetterly's 'Hidden Figures: The Story of the African-American Women Who Helped Win the Space Race' is published in 2016, featuring Dorothy Vaughan.

name: Henry Hampton
description: Filmmaker (1940–1998), creator and executive producer of the Eyes on the Prize documentary series; founder of the Boston production company Blackside.

name: Household of Ruth
aliases: Household of Ruth of the GUOOF
description: Women's auxiliary of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows in America, founded by Patrick H. Reason in 1858; open to Odd Fellows and related women; members (called inmates) receive sick and funeral benefits; over 800 branches with 40,000 members by 1893.

name: Harold Pierce
description: African American entrepreneur (August 11, 1917 - March 8, 1988) who founded the Harold's Chicken Shack chain in Chicago on June 22, 1950; retired to Beaverville, Illinois in the early 1980s.

name: Herman Hartman
description: Father of Hermene Hartman; the first Black Pepsi-Cola distributor in the United States; from Houma, Louisiana, lived in Chicago from about age 12.

name: Harvard station opens (November 3, 1906)
description: Harvard station opens November 3, 1906, on the Englewood branch of the Chicago 'L' at Harvard Avenue and 63rd Street; distinct from CTL-E-1014 (the station).

name: Harvard station closes (February 9, 1992)
description: Harvard station closes February 9, 1992, in CTA budget-driven service cuts; distinct from CTL-E-1014 (the station).

name: Harris B. Gaines
description: Husband of Irene McCoy Gaines; father with her of two sons, Charles and Harris Jr.

name: Hachette v. Internet Archive ruling (2023-03-25)
description: U.S. District Court (S.D.N.Y.) rules the Internet Archive's controlled digital lending constitutes copyright infringement; affirmed by the Second Circuit in September 2024.

name: Harvard University
description: Ivy League university in Cambridge, Massachusetts; Latanya Sweeney is Daniel Paul Professor of the Practice of Government and Technology there and founded its Public Interest Tech Lab.

name: HBCU Library Alliance
description: The HBCU Library Alliance is a consortium supporting the libraries of historically Black colleges and universities, founded in 2002. Beginning in 2005, the Alliance partnered with Cornell University Library in a Mellon Foundation-funded project to build HBCU digital collections: across grants of $450,000 and then $375,000, the partnership trained 23 HBCU library staff and produced a searchable group of more than 7,000 digital images from the archives of 20 HBCUs. CultureTechLens's CTL-DR-PRESERVE-001 research cites the partnership as real progress in HBCU digitization — and, simultaneously, as a measure of how little had been digitized before. The Alliance also appears in CTL's preservation research alongside Harvard in the HBCU Digital Library Trust, a public digital library effort for HBCU materials.

name: HBCU Digital Library Trust
description: The HBCU Digital Library Trust is a digital-preservation consortium launched in 2023 as a four-year project, funded by a $6 million grant from Harvard's Legacy of Slavery initiative and operated by the HBCU Library Alliance in partnership with Harvard Library and the AUC Woodruff Library. It expands digital access to the history of Black academia — HBCU archives, student newspapers, yearbooks, photographs, and records — through a public digital library. By 2024 it represented more than 30 HBCUs and had added over 16,500 digitized items, against a stated target of all 107 HBCUs; the AUC Woodruff Library also received a $500,000 MacArthur Foundation grant to expand the digitization work. Its program director is Andrea Jackson Gavin. CultureTechLens's preservation research flags the structural risk plainly: a four-year grant is not a permanent endowment, and post-grant sustainability remains the initiative's open question.

name: Henry Brown
description: Chicago Defender cartoonist who took over Bungleton Green in 1929, shifting it to a soap-opera-style serial after a stroke hindered creator Leslie Rogers.

name: Hiram Maxim
description: Inventor and industrialist; Lewis Latimer worked with Maxim at the U.S. Electric Lighting Company from 1881 on carbon filaments, collaborating with Joseph V. Nichols.

name: How's Your Evening So Far?
description: 2000 track by Josh Wink, credited to Wink Featuring Lil Louis, that heavily sampled 'French Kiss'; peaked at No. 3 on the dance chart.

name: Hal Fruth
description: Business partner of inventor Otis Boykin; together they established Boykin-Fruth, Inc. after Boykin's stint as a research engineer at P.J. Nilsen Research Labs.

name: Houston, Texas
description: Home city of the Houston Forward Times and of publisher Karen Carter Richards (Houston native since infancy); home of KCOH and its historic Third Ward 'Looking Glass' studio.

name: Hawaii Rainbow Warriors football
aliases: Hawaii Rainbow Warriors; University of Hawaii football
description: Football program of the University of Hawaii at Manoa; Norm Chow was head coach 2012-2015 (10-36).

name: Herbert 'Herb J' Jackson
description: Founding member of the Chicago acid-house group Phuture (1985); co-writer of 'Acid Tracks' (1987).

name: He's My Light
description: Gospel song composed by Lucy Smith Collier; a hit for the Roberta Martin Singers.

name: Harvard Society of Fellows
description: Harvard University fellowship body; Rediet Abebe was a Junior Fellow.

name: Hewlett-Packard
description: Technology company whose computer division Roy L. Clay Sr. helped found in 1965; the HP 2116A was its first computer.

name: Hossein Eslambolchi
description: Telecommunications inventor; co-invented text-to-donate technology with Marian Croak (U.S. Patent 7,715,368), which raised roughly $130,000 for Hurricane Katrina relief and more than $43 million for Haiti earthquake relief.

description: Record label launched by members of the Hot Mix 5 in the mid-1980s; started by Mickey Oliver with Kenny Jason and Ralphi Rosario.

name: HipHopWired
description: Hip-hop news website in the Moguldom Media Group network. Acquired by Urban One's iONE Digital in 2017.

name: HBCU Homecoming
description: HBCU Homecoming is the multi-day ritual of return for alumni and community at historically Black colleges and universities. Each fall it brings tens of thousands of alumni, family, and community members back to campus for marching bands, step shows, sunrise tailgates, and parades — with the football game, in CultureTechLens's documented account, almost beside the point. CTL's thin brief CTL-TB-000025, 'Homecoming: The Black College Ritual,' frames it as the family reunion of Black institutional life: generations of graduates returning to the place that made them, showing current students what they can become. From Chicago, alumni chapters organize buses and flights every October. CTL has documented the ritual in a three-part Short series (2026) and in coverage of the 100th GHOE, the Greatest Homecoming on Earth.

name: Harold Washington Library Center
description: The Harold Washington Library Center is the main branch of the Chicago Public Library. It is home to YOUmedia, the library's teen digital-learning program, which opened in 2009; Chicago rapper Noname spent time as a teen in the YOUMedia project at the Harold Washington Library. The building houses CPL's Special Collections Division, cited in a finding aid as the holder of the Kuumba collection; a Smithsonian Archives of American Art survey also places the George Cleveland Hall Branch Archives there — 28 linear feet of records dating from 1932 to the 1970s, including remnants of the Special Negro Collection.

name: Hot Buttered Soul
description: Hot Buttered Soul is the second studio album by Isaac Hayes, released in July 1969 on Enterprise Records, Stax Records’ subsidiary, as Stax rushed to rebuild its catalogue. The album holds only four tracks across some 45 minutes: a roughly 12-minute reading of “Walk On By,” the original “Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic,” “One Woman,” and an 18-minute closing treatment of “By the Time I Get to Phoenix” framed by a spoken monologue. Where soul albums were still built as collections of three-minute singles, Hayes stretched four songs into long, orchestrated statements, and the record became a landmark of album-oriented soul. It spent ten weeks at number one on Billboard’s R&B albums chart, peaked at number eight on the Billboard 200, and was certified gold by the RIAA in December 1969.

name: Halle Bailey
description: American singer-songwriter and actress, born Halle Lynn Bailey on March 27, 2000, in Atlanta, Georgia, and raised in Mableton, who first reached audiences as one half of the sister duo Chloe x Halle. Posting covers to YouTube as teenagers, she and her sister Chloe Bailey caught Beyoncé's attention with their rendition of Pretty Hurts and signed to Beyoncé's Parkwood Entertainment in 2016. The duo released The Kids Are Alright (2018) and Ungodly Hour (2020), earning five Grammy nominations together, while Bailey acted in the sitcom Grown-ish from 2018 to 2022. Her solo breakthrough came on screen and record at once: she starred as Ariel in Disney's live-action The Little Mermaid (2023), played Nettie in The Color Purple (2023), and released her debut solo single Angel in 2023, which earned her first solo Grammy nomination, for Best R&B Song. Her debut solo studio album, Love?... or Something Like It, followed on October 24, 2025, marking her step from celebrated duo member and Disney lead to a solo recording artist in her own right.

name: Huey P. Newton
aliases: Huey Percy Newton; Dr. Huey P. Newton
description: Huey Percy Newton was born in Monroe, Louisiana, in 1942 and raised in Oakland, California, where he graduated from high school, by his own account, without having learned to read — then taught himself, beginning with Plato, and went on through Merritt College and law study to a doctorate in social philosophy from the University of California, Santa Cruz, in 1980. In Oakland in 1966, with Bobby Seale, he co-founded the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense, drafted its Ten-Point Program, and served as minister of defense. The party married armed self-defense rhetoric and community survival programs — free breakfasts for children, health clinics, and schools — into a Black Power politics that spread to chapters nationwide and drew intense federal surveillance and repression. Newton's 1967 arrest in the shooting death of an Oakland police officer made 'Free Huey' an international rallying cry; his manslaughter conviction was overturned and he was freed in 1970. Later years brought exile in Cuba from 1974 to 1977, further trials ending without conviction, internal party collapse, and addiction. He was shot and killed in Oakland on August 22, 1989, aged forty-seven. His flowers are complicated and honest: CTL honors the Oakland organizer who fed children and built a political vocabulary of self-determination, while recording the violence and decline that shadowed his final years.

name: Hidden Figures
description: Hidden Figures, directed by Theodore Melfi and written by Melfi with Allison Schroeder from Margot Lee Shetterly's nonfiction book, was released by 20th Century Fox in limited release on December 25, 2016, and wide on January 6, 2017. It tells the story of Katherine Johnson, Dorothy Vaughan, and Mary Jackson — the Black women mathematicians whose calculations at NASA's Langley center carried the early space program while segregation ordered their working lives. The film was nominated for three Academy Awards — Best Picture, Best Adapted Screenplay, and Best Supporting Actress for Octavia Spencer — and won the Screen Actors Guild Award for its cast's ensemble performance. A commercial success at a reported $236 million worldwide on a $25 million budget, it moved its three subjects from specialist history into the general curriculum. Unusually for this wave, the graph already holds the underlying record: Johnson (CTL-E-1065), Vaughan (CTL-E-1036), and Jackson (CTL-E-1077) hold Person records, and the book's publication holds an Event record (CTL-E-3667). This film record completes the set — the dramatization filed beside the women themselves.

name: Hue
description: Hue was a pocket-sized entertainment magazine launched in Chicago in November 1953 by the Johnson Publishing Company, modeled on the digest format that had made Jet a success two years earlier. Where Jet carried the news, Hue, a monthly, concentrated on entertainment, fashion, and celebrities — the public, pleasurable surface of Black life in the 1950s — with photo-led coverage of performers, nightlife, and style. An early issue, volume 1, number 11, is dated June 16, 1954, and is held today by the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture; a copy of the first issue, November 1953, survives in the Lomazow magazine collection exhibited at the Grolier Club. Hue ceased publication in 1959, after roughly six years. It remains the least documented of John H. Johnson's thirteen magazines: no circulation figure for it was verified in this research pass, and its short run is precisely what makes its surviving issues valuable evidence of the Johnson formula at its most experimental.

name: Horace J. Blackwell
description: Horace J. Blackwell was a Fort Worth, Texas, clothing merchant who became a pioneering Black magazine publisher. In 1942 he founded The World's Messenger, a true-confessions magazine whose stories were written in the dialect of Southern working-class Black readers. In 1946 he launched Negro Achievements, a photojournalistic magazine of Black accomplishment published through his Good Publishing Company and built with women in leading editorial roles, including editorial director Adelle Martin Jackson and Beatrice Pringle. Blackwell died in the late 1940s — the sources consulted divide between 1948 and 1949, and this record does not choose between them — and in 1950 his magazines and company were sold to George Levitan, under whom Negro Achievements became Sepia (CTL-E-5514). Almost nothing of Blackwell's personal life survives in the national record consulted for this packet, and that thinness is stated rather than padded: the record is staged Provisional, with its upgrade path named.

name: Harriet Tubman
description: Harriet Tubman is an American jazz-based power trio formed in New York City in 1998 by guitarist Brandon Ross, bassist Melvin Gibbs, and drummer J.T. Lewis, named for the abolitionist Harriet Tubman (CTL-E-1565) as an emblem of liberation. The band's music fuses electronic jazz, rock, funk, dub, and doom metal into what NPR called “black music at its best.” Its discography runs from I Am a Man (1998) and Prototype (2000) through Ascension (2011), Araminta (2017, with trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith — Araminta being Tubman's birth name), and The Terror End of Beauty (2018). Electrical Field of Love (2026, Pi Recordings) — the subject of CTL Short #55 — adds vocalist Georgia Anne Muldrow to the trio. This record is the BAND; the abolitionist's own record stands separately at CTL-E-1565.

name: Hannibal Buress
description: Hannibal Buress, born Hannibal Amir Buress on February 4, 1983, is an American comedian, actor, and writer raised in Chicago's Austin neighborhood. After Steinmetz College Prep he attended Southern Illinois University Carbondale for four years without graduating, and began performing stand-up there in 2002. He wrote for Saturday Night Live (2009–2010) and 30 Rock, released the albums My Name Is Hannibal (2010) and Animal Furnace (2012), and was named to Variety's Ten Comics to Watch in 2010. Buress co-starred on The Eric Andre Show (2012–2020) and played Lincoln Rice on Broad City (2014–2019). On October 16, 2014, a stand-up routine in Philadelphia in which he called attention to the sexual-assault allegations against Bill Cosby went viral and is widely credited with returning those allegations to national attention. He has since headlined multiple Netflix and Comedy Central specials while keeping Chicago as a creative home base.

name: Higher Ground Productions
description: Higher Ground Productions is the media production company founded in 2018 by former President Barack Obama (CTL-E-0079) and former First Lady Michelle Obama (CTL-E-5574) — the exact name the company's own record and its trade coverage carry. It launched in May 2018 with a multi-year Netflix deal to produce scripted and unscripted film and television projects that lift up diverse voices; its first film, American Factory (2019), won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. A June 2019 Spotify partnership created its audio arm, Higher Ground Audio, which premiered The Michelle Obama Podcast in July 2020; the audio business moved to Audible in 2022, and in March 2025 the company announced IMO, the podcast Michelle Obama hosts with her brother Craig Robinson (the show's record is CTL-E-5594). After a Netflix partnership that produced 24 projects by trade counts, Higher Ground announced in April 2026 that it would transition into an independent production company working across multiple studios. IMO's record in this graph has carried the produced_by credit to this company as a blocked edge since Shorts Wave 3; this record is the endpoint.

name: Hep
description: Hep was a Black-audience entertainment magazine published in Fort Worth, Texas, by the Good Publishing Company, the house behind Sepia. In the standard account of the company, George Levitan — the Fort Worth merchant who bought Horace J. Blackwell's magazines and the Good Publishing Company in 1950 and ran the firm until his death in 1976 — published Hep alongside the companion title Jive as part of the same Black-audience list that carried Sepia and Bronze Thrills. Hep belonged to the entertainment side of that list rather than to Sepia's photojournalism of Black achievement: it was a fan-and-features magazine for Black readers in the decades when Good Publishing stood as Ebony's Fort Worth rival. Direct documentation of the title is thin: the fullest surviving traces are the company history that names it among Levitan's magazines and physical issues in the collectors' market, including an issue dated May 1972, which places Hep still in publication more than two decades after the Levitan purchase. No library catalog entry, circulation figure, or founding date for Hep was verified at staging, and none is asserted here.

name: Hot Boys
description: The Hot Boys are the Uptown New Orleans hip-hop group formed in 1997 on Cash Money Records, composed of B.G., Lil Wayne, Juvenile and Turk. The quartet first appeared together on B.G.'s It's All on U, Vol. 1 and released its debut album, Get It How U Live!, in 1997 to regional success. After Cash Money's 1998 distribution deal with Universal Records, the group released Guerrilla Warfare (July 27, 1999), produced entirely by Mannie Fresh: it debuted at number five on the Billboard 200 and number one on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, sold 142,000 copies in its first week, and was certified platinum by the RIAA. Its singles 'We On Fire' and 'I Need a Hot Girl' carried the Cash Money sound nationally. The group then came apart: Juvenile, Turk and B.G. left Cash Money, citing financial mismanagement, leaving Lil Wayne as the only member still signed; a third album, Let 'Em Burn (2003), was assembled from recordings made between 1998 and 2000. All four members reunited on record on a 2012 remix of Turk's 'Zip It,' and a full stage reunion remained elusive for two more decades.

name: Herman Roberts
description: Herman Roberts (born 1924, Beggs, Oklahoma; died February 1, 2021) moved to Chicago at twelve in the Great Migration, attended Burke Elementary and Englewood High School, and built one of Black Chicago's great hospitality empires from a taxicab fleet that reached thirty-five cabs. In the early 1950s he opened the Lucky Spot lounge, then the Roberts Show Lounge in his former cab garage, booking Nina Simone, Dinah Washington, Sarah Vaughan, Sammy Davis Jr., Sam Cooke, Redd Foxx, Moms Mabley, and Dick Gregory. His first Roberts Motel opened in 1960 on 63rd Street and grew to eight motels; the sixth, in 1970, was a 250-room complex, and the Roberts Motel 500 Room hosted the official kickoff of Harold Washington's mayoral campaign. The HistoryMakers calls him the nation's foremost African American hotel and motel owner. He also held an Oklahoma ranch where he struck oil in 1981. Congressman Danny K. Davis entered a tribute in the Congressional Record on March 18, 2021.

name: Homestead Grays
description: The Homestead Grays were a Negro league baseball club rooted in Homestead, Pennsylvania, the steel town outside Pittsburgh whose mill workers first fielded the team. Organized in 1910 and taken in hand by player, manager, and eventual owner Cumberland Posey, the Grays played profitably as an independent club, joined the short-lived American Negro League in 1929, and fielded eastern championship teams in 1930 and 1931. After Depression-era lean years and a failed East-West League, Posey brought the club into the reorganized Negro National League, where it became a full member and built a dynasty around catcher Josh Gibson and first baseman Buck Leonard. The Grays won nine consecutive league pennants and three Negro World Series titles, split their home dates between Pittsburgh and Washington, and outlasted the league itself, playing two final independent seasons before disbanding after 1950.

name: Hiram Revels
aliases: Hiram Rhodes Revels; Hiram R. Revels
description: Hiram Rhodes Revels, born free in Fayetteville, North Carolina, on September 27, 1827, was a barber, an African Methodist Episcopal minister ordained in 1845, and a Civil War recruiter who helped raise two Black regiments in Maryland and served as a chaplain at Vicksburg. Settling in Natchez, Mississippi, after the war, he was elected alderman in 1868 and then to the Mississippi state senate. On February 25, 1870, after the Senate rejected a challenge to his credentials, Revels took the oath as the first African American United States senator, filling the seat Jefferson Davis had vacated, and became the first Black member of Congress. In his single year he argued for racial equality, opposed segregated schools in the District of Columbia, and pressed the case of Black workers barred from the Washington Navy Yard. He later served as Mississippi's interim secretary of state and as president of Alcorn University, and returned to ministry and teaching before his death in 1901.

name: Hezly Rivera
description: Hezly Rivera, born 4 June 2008 in Hackensack, New Jersey to Dominican parents and raised in Oradell, New Jersey, is an American artistic gymnast. She began gymnastics at five, moved with her family to Texas in 2021 to train at the World Olympic Gymnastics Academy under Valeri Liukin, and in 2023 won the U.S. junior national title and Junior World Championships team and floor exercise silver medals. At Paris 2024, at sixteen the youngest athlete on the whole of Team USA, she was a member of the “Golden Girls” team that won Olympic gold. She describes herself as proud to be Latina and Dominican American, and was a TIME Latino Leaders honoree in 2024. She won the U.S. senior national all-around championship in 2025 and repeated in Phoenix in August 2026 with a two-day total of 111.950 — the first American woman other than Simone Biles to go back-to-back since Jordyn Wieber in 2011–12 — while recovering from a hamstring injury. She is committed to Louisiana State University for 2027–30.

name: Herman Wrice
description: Herman Wrice (1939–2000) was a Philadelphia community organizer who became one of the best-known grassroots anti-drug activists in the United States. Born in a small West Virginia coal-mining town and raised in Chester and in Philadelphia's Mantua neighborhood, he graduated from Overbrook High School in 1957 and spent years running youth programs in Mantua. In 1988, as crack cocaine devastated the neighborhood, he organized Mantua Against Drugs (MAD) and developed the 'Wrice Process' of direct action: residents marching on street corners, posting 'Dealer of the Week' wanted posters, and demolishing crack houses — famously wearing a white hard hat provided by Mayor Wilson Goode. His methods were adopted by communities across Philadelphia and, through his work as a Department of Justice emissary in the 1990s, by some three hundred communities nationwide. Wrice died of a heart attack in Florida on 10 March 2000, the day before he was to lead an anti-drug march in Fort Lauderdale.

name: Hosea Sanders
description: Hosea Sanders is an Arkadelphia, Arkansas native and a Chicago television anchor, entertainment reporter, and program host who has worked at ABC 7 Chicago since 1994. A 1978 graduate of Henderson State University, he learned journalism there as co-editor of The Oracle campus newspaper, helped create a news department at campus radio station KSWH-FM from the ground up, and worked at local station KVRC and for Arkadelphia newspapers while still a student. His first television job, at KARK-TV in Little Rock, became the foundation he still calls his touchstone for quality broadcasting. At ABC 7 — WLS-TV, the station he describes as his home for more than thirty years — his work has included anchoring, entertainment reporting, and hosting station programming for Chicago audiences. Henderson State's August 2025 alumni profile, published as an interview with Sanders himself, calls him a twenty-one-time Emmy Award winner, records his Silver Circle Award from the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences for his contributions to broadcasting in Chicago, and notes his appointment to Henderson's Board of Visitors and his continuing campus visits. His advice to young journalists is to work harder than anyone around them — and, as he puts it, not to be like him, but to be better.

name: Hakeem Jeffries
aliases: Hakeem Sekou Jeffries; Hakeem S. Jeffries
description: Hakeem Jeffries is an American politician and attorney representing New York's Eighth Congressional District in the United States House of Representatives, where Congress.gov records his service from 2013 to the present across the 113th through 119th Congresses. Born in Brooklyn and raised in Crown Heights, he is a product of New York City public schools and a graduate of Midwood High School. He earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Binghamton University, a master's degree in public policy from Georgetown University, and a law degree from New York University School of Law, where he graduated magna cum laude and served on the Law Review. After clerking for a federal district judge and practicing at Paul, Weiss and as counsel at Viacom and CBS, he served six years in the New York State Assembly before entering Congress. House Democrats unanimously elected him their leader in 2022 and again in 2024, making him the highest-ranking Democrat in the House; he previously chaired the House Democratic Caucus and served as whip of the Congressional Black Caucus. In January 2026 he led the discharge-petition effort that passed a three-year extension of Affordable Care Act tax credits through the House.

name: Hank Aaron
aliases: Henry Louis Aaron; Hammerin' Hank; Hank Aaron (baseball)
description: Henry Louis Aaron, born February 5, 1934, in Mobile, Alabama, was the baseball player who broke Babe Ruth's career home-run record and held it for more than three decades. Raised in the segregated South, he played for the semipro Mobile Black Bears and the Indianapolis Clowns of the Negro American League before signing with the Braves organization. He reached the major leagues with Milwaukee in 1954, won the National League Most Valuable Player award and a World Series title in 1957, won batting titles in 1956 and 1959, and earned three Gold Glove Awards. The Braves moved to Atlanta after the 1965 season. Pursuing Ruth's record, Aaron and his family endured racist threats and harassment. On April 8, 1974, he hit his 715th home run. Traded to the Milwaukee Brewers, he retired after 1976 and later worked as a Braves executive and civil-rights supporter. He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1982 and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2002. He died on January 22, 2021, in Atlanta.

name: Henry McNeal Turner
description: Henry McNeal Turner, born free in 1834 in Newberry Courthouse, South Carolina, to Sarah Greer and Hardy Turner, became one of the most influential Black leaders of late nineteenth-century Georgia. Educated with help from lawyers at an Abbeville law firm where he worked as a janitor, he was licensed as a Methodist preacher in 1853 and joined the African Methodist Episcopal Church, holding pastorates in Baltimore and Washington, D.C. In 1863 he helped organize the First Regiment of U.S. Colored Troops and served as its chaplain, the first African American chaplain in United States Army history. After the Civil War he organized AME congregations and the Republican Party across Georgia, was elected to the Georgia legislature in 1868, was expelled with the other Black members, and reclaimed his seat in 1870. Elected the twelfth bishop of the AME Church in 1880, he was the first AME bishop to ordain a woman. Disillusioned by Jim Crow, he became the era's leading advocate of emigration to Africa, founding newspapers and organizing 1895–1896 voyages to Liberia. He died May 8, 1915, in Windsor, Ontario.

name: Henry Ossawa Tanner
description: Henry Ossawa Tanner was an American painter born June 21, 1859, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to Benjamin and Sarah Tanner, and raised in Philadelphia, where the family relocated. He enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, among the first African Americans to do so, and studied with Thomas Eakins. In 1891 he moved to Paris and studied at the Académie Julian, taking up permanent residence in France during the 1890s and competing in the annual Paris Salons, where he found success and international renown unprecedented for an African American artist. His reputation was founded on paintings of religious subjects, including The Resurrection of Lazarus in 1896 and Nicodemus Visiting Christ in 1899, but for most Americans he is known for the early genre painting The Banjo Lesson, painted in 1893, showing an elderly African American man teaching a boy to play the banjo. He was elected a member of the National Academy of Design in 1910, and in 1923 the French government made him a chevalier of the Legion of Honor. He died May 25, 1937, in Paris, aged 77.
